summary:
Legal gender recognition in Chile rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. People aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; those under 14 cannot use the law, though the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and the ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, but the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres; the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.
tangentialFactors:
A Chilean advocacy group's annual report judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTQ rights, citing stalled equality and trans-rights legislation, the rise of the ultra-right and government inaction. Movilh, the Chilean LGBT integration movement, published its 24th Annual Human Rights Report on sexual and gender diversity covering 2025, which stands as the most current domestic accounting of conditions.

The F&M Global Barometers country profile for Chile publishes composite scores for LGBT rights perception, including a Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index; the specific values are not reproduced in the sources reviewed here.

Article 373 of the Penal Code, covering offences to morals and good customs, was historically used by police to harass people for holding hands in public. A 2015 Movilh report noted that for the first time in seven years no police abuses against LGBT people were reported, crediting the Carabineros Human Rights Department, but recent reporting on the article's use is not available in the sources reviewed.
localsOnly:
Institutional discrimination inside the national police force is in litigation. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros alleging she was relegated to administrative tasks, that her private life was exposed without consent, and that support was denied to her.

Education protections are extensive. A Ministry of Education circular of April 2017, Rights of girls, boys and trans students in the field of education, requires schools nationwide to provide bathroom and shower facilities respecting the gender identity of trans students, alongside guarantees of social name use and gender-conforming uniforms, and non-compliance is sanctionable. Related measures include the 2009 General Law of Education, the 2011 School Violence Law requiring Good School Coexistence Committees, the 2013 Superintendence of Education handbook on non-discriminatory treatment, the 2015 to 2018 National School Coexistence Policy, the School Inclusion law effective March 2016, and Law 21,430 of 15 March 2022, the first regulation explicitly protecting LGBTIQA+ children and adolescents, including non-discrimination on sex characteristics and the right to develop gender identity, with state bodies obliged to create programmes on sexual rights and diversity.

The domestic movement's institutional record includes the anti-discrimination law, inclusive questions in the 2012 census, the 'El amor es amor' marriage campaign, and Comuna Diversa local-level work with regional branches.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the Constitutional Court's April 2025 inapplicability ruling on the 14-year threshold will be generalised to other cases, or whether the court has since ruled on under-14 access more broadly. The sources reviewed treat it as case-specific.

Unresolved: whether the national clinical guidelines contemplated by Circular 7 of June 2024 have since been published, and how the deferral suggestion is applied in practice across regions.

Unresolved: the practical reach of the November 2025 defunding of the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program, including which services the Ministry of Health-run successor covers and at which centres.

Unresolved: enforcement data for the Zamudio Law and the hate-crime aggravating circumstance, including conviction rates in cases with anti-trans motivation; no court statistics appear in the sources reviewed.

Unresolved: whether the CEI 57 commission's non-binding recommendations have been converted into legislation or regulatory action, and the status of the school circular it proposes to repeal.

Not sourced: any systematic reporting on border screening of transgender travellers, mismatch between passport markers and presentation at Chilean ports of entry, or the handling of foreign visitors whose documents reflect a gender marker obtained abroad.
